questions.q: Why does this lesson say a group that only reviews and approves other teams' architecture proposals isn't really a Cloud Center of Excellence?
options: That function is essentially a gate wearing a more ambitious name, and a group whose entire job is reviewing others' work hasn't built anything itself
Review boards are illegal under most compliance frameworks
A CCoE is required by Azure and AWS to exist as a technical service, not a team of people
Reviewing proposals is actually the fastest possible governance mechanism
questions.explain: A pure review function is a gate in Lesson 19's terms; it provokes the same shadow-IT response and doesn't produce anything an excellent team could point to and reuse.

questions.q: What does a real CCoE concretely own, according to this lesson?
options: Only the right to reject non-compliant resource requests
A quarterly newsletter summarizing cloud spend
The shared Terraform module catalog, the policy baseline, and the landing zone itself
Nothing technical — only meeting schedules and sign-off forms
questions.explain: A functioning CCoE is a platform team: it builds and maintains the reusable modules, the policy baseline from Lesson 17, and the landing zone foundation from Chapter 2.

questions.q: Why does consuming a CCoE-built storage-account module satisfy the policy baseline 'by construction'?
options: The module bypasses policy enforcement entirely for trusted teams
Policy enforcement only applies to resources built by hand, not by modules
A CCoE-maintained module is pre-built to already include the required encryption, logging, and tagging, so a team consuming it is compliant without a separate review step
Terraform modules cannot be checked by Azure Policy at all
questions.explain: Because the shared module already encodes the baseline's requirements, a team that consumes it gets compliance by default — the guardrail pattern applied to tooling itself, rather than compliance verified after the fact.

questions.q: Why does this lesson treat training and enablement as real CCoE output rather than a side activity?
options: A module catalog only pays off if teams know it exists and know how to use it — without documentation and onboarding, teams reinvent what already exists
Training is only needed once, during a CCoE's first year of existence
Enablement work is actually the responsibility of each product team's own manager
Documentation has no measurable effect on whether modules get adopted
questions.explain: Without office hours, documentation, and onboarding, teams who don't know the shared modules exist will quietly rebuild what the CCoE already built, so enablement is what makes the module catalog's value actually land.

questions.q: What honest test does this lesson suggest for telling whether a CCoE is functioning as a platform team or as a review committee?
options: How many people currently sit on the CCoE
How large the CCoE's annual budget is compared to other teams
Whether the CCoE has a published charter document
Whether a product team, when it needed a compliant resource last quarter, consumed something the CCoE built or waited for the CCoE to approve something the team built itself
questions.explain: If teams are consuming CCoE-built modules, it's functioning as a platform team; if they're waiting on approval for work they did themselves, it's a review committee with a better title, and the fix is shifting effort toward building reusable infrastructure.
